fields.meta_title: Restaurant Survey Builder for Tables and Delivery | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a restaurant survey for dine-in and delivery guests that flags missing items, compares locations, and keeps every answer in your database.
fields.h1: Build a Restaurant Survey That Reaches the Manager on Shift
fields.hero_description: Create a restaurant survey diners scan from the check, with each low score sent to the manager while they are still there.
fields.features_heading: What a Restaurant Survey Needs to Do
fields.features_subheading: Each part below follows a shift: the table that paid, the order that left the kitchen, and the menu that changes next season.
fields.feature_1:
Questions written for diners

Describe your restaurant and how you serve. Emergent drafts restaurant survey questions on food, service, and wait times, worded for a guest reading on a phone before leaving.
fields.feature_2:
A link tied to each table or order

Print a QR code on the check or text a link after delivery. Each link carries the table or order number, and every answer arrives already matched to the exact visit it rates.
fields.feature_3:
Alerts while guests are still seated

Set the score that counts as a problem. A rating at or below it sends the manager on duty a Slack message or an email with the check number, the score, and the comment.
fields.feature_4:
Every location on one dashboard

Run one survey at all your locations and compare their averages week by week. Sort the results by any question to find the dining room or kitchen that trails the others.
fields.feature_5:
Menu tests that end in a decision

Ask guests who ordered a new dish whether they would order it again. Set how many answers count and the share of yes votes that keeps a dish, then see which dishes pass.
fields.feature_6:
Answers and code you keep

Store every response in a database you own, with no cap on how many people answer each month. Export the full code to your GitHub repository on paid plans and build on it.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Restaurant Surveys Wired Into Service
fields.tab_content_1:
A low score reaches the floor before the table leaves

Every check at the bistro carries a QR code with the table number in the link. Diners rate the food, the service, and the wait out of 5, then add a comment if they like. Any rating of 2 or lower sends the floor manager a Slack message while the party is still seated.
fields.tab_content_2:
Fries missing from the bag, flagged within the hour

Thirty minutes after the driver marks an order delivered, the pizza shop texts the customer through Twilio. The text asks whether the food arrived hot, whether anything was missing, and for a rating out of 5. When an answer names a missing item, the kitchen lead gets an email with the order number and the item.
fields.tab_content_3:
Six kitchens, one wait time out of line

All six locations of a taco chain ask the same questions, and the answers roll into one weekly view. Last week 412 guests replied. The Eastside wait averaged 2.8 out of 5, while every other location scored 4.1 or higher, and the operations lead opened its comments first.
fields.tab_content_4:
Fifty votes decide each spring dish

Four new dishes went on the spring menu at a neighborhood cafe. Guests who ordered one get a single question on their receipt link: would you order it again? After 50 answers per dish, any dish with fewer than 30 yes votes comes off. The miso salmon bowl stopped at 19 and was replaced.

fields.howto_title: How to Run a Restaurant Survey
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to run a restaurant survey that guests finish and managers act on, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Decide who acts on each answer
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Ask about one thing per question
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Pass the table or order number
fields.howto_step_1_des: Before writing a question, name the person who will act on it. A low service score on a Friday night belongs with the floor manager. A missing item belongs with the kitchen. A question nobody owns ends up as a number in a monthly report.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Guests answer on a phone, often while reaching for a coat. Completion drops as surveys get longer, and customers put up with length less than employees do. Stick to a few ratings and one open box, and cut any question you would not act on.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Rating the food and the service in one question gives a number nobody can use. Split them, and keep the wording neutral as well. Ask how the wait was, not how much the diner enjoyed the quick service, because loaded wording pushes answers one way.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Put the table, check, or order number in the survey link. Each answer then sits next to the visit it describes. A complaint about cold pasta traces back to the night and the station that cooked it.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Set a threshold worth interrupting for
fields.howto_step_5_des: Pick the score that should pull a manager away mid-shift, such as a service score under 3. Set it too high and managers start ignoring alerts. Set it too low and a bad night passes with nobody hearing about it until the reviews show up.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Hold the wording steady across sites
fields.howto_step_6_des: Restaurant survey examples often mix questions freely, but a chain cannot compare locations that way. Give every location identical questions in the same order. If one site needs its own question, add it after the shared ones so the averages still line up.
fields.howto_step_7_des: An average points to the problem; the comments explain it. Each week, open the lowest-scoring question at each location and read every comment under it before the staff meeting. Quote one or two to the team that owns the fix.

plan.angle: The top 10 is long question lists (Zonka, Formbricks, SevenRooms, Momos), one SurveyMonkey template and restaurant-tech vendors pitching their own guest platforms. None shows where the answers go once a guest taps submit. This page gives the questions a restaurant should ask and shows four restaurant surveys wired to the shift: a QR code on the check that pings the floor manager while the table is still seated, a text after delivery that catches missing items by order number, one survey compared across six locations, and a new-dish test that decides what stays on the menu. The guest-satisfaction sibling owns hotel stays; the customer-feedback sibling owns general feedback; this page owns the dining room, the delivery bag and the menu.
tab_stories: A bistro prints a QR code on every check, guests rate food, service and the wait out of 5, and any rating of 2 or lower sends the floor manager a Slack message with the table number while the guests are still seated.
A pizza shop texts each delivery customer 30 minutes after the driver marks the order delivered, and any answer that says an item was missing reaches the kitchen lead by email with the order number.
A taco chain runs the same survey at all six locations, and a weekly table of 412 answers shows one location's wait averaging 2.8 while every other location scores 4.1 or higher.
A cafe testing four spring dishes asks each guest who ordered one whether they would order it again, and after 50 answers per dish the miso salmon bowl sits at 38% and comes off the menu.
